headline: AI memory system learns what to forget to improve recall, now open-source
summary: A new open-source memory system for AI agents, Lorekeeper, focuses on prioritizing useful information rather than total recall, mirroring human memory patterns.
details: The traditional view of AI memory aimed for perfect, total recall, saving every conversation and detail. However, this approach often leads to an overwhelming amount of data, making it difficult for AI agents to find relevant information.

The developer of Lorekeeper, an open-source memory system, shifted focus from merely storing everything to intelligently knowing what to keep. This design is inspired by how human memory naturally prioritizes important experiences and information.

Lorekeeper incorporates a feedback loop where an AI agent can mark a memory as 'useful' each time it's accessed. Memories that are frequently used are retained and promoted, while less relevant information gradually fades, preventing clutter.

This selective retention proved highly effective. In one instance, an agent remembered a specific, obscure debugging session from weeks prior because the memory had consistently proven useful across multiple interactions, surprising the developer.

The project emphasizes that the goal for AI memory isn't perfect recall, but rather the ability to discern and retain what truly matters. Lorekeeper is available open-source under the Apache 2.0 license and can be installed via pip.

headline: I gave Claude Code a team of AI agents, transforming my role to conductor
summary: After teaching Claude Code to "think before it codes," the author scaled the concept by having a single orchestrator AI manage specialist subagents, parallelizing development tasks. This shifts the human role from coding or detailed prompting to workflow tunin
details: The initial problem with AI coding assistants like Claude was process, not intelligence. The author previously developed a "/wizard" prompt to force disciplined senior engineer habits: reading code, defining acceptance criteria, writing tests first, then minimal code.

This version one approach made Claude a fantastic individual contributor but was still limited to one pair of hands. The new version two shifts the mental model from "make Claude a senior developer" to "make Claude a senior architect who runs a team."

Concretely, v2 uses a main-thread orchestrator that never writes code itself. It fans out work to specialist subagents, each in its own isolated git worktree, building in parallel and driving multiple pull requests through automated review.

This setup allows the author to describe a feature, walk away, and return to find an engineering team had been shipping while they slept. The v1 discipline is preserved underneath, with the team only spinning up for complex tasks.

The author also automated the issue creation process. An "issue-maintainer" agent now takes a one-line idea and produces a structured issue with clear titles, acceptance criteria, and consistent labels, improving consistency and downstream efficiency.
